# Smelting iron with coke (`coke_iron`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: needs blast_furnace_cast_iron; helped by coal_mining, atmospheric_engine, refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: Raw coal spoils iron with sulphur and cakes in the furnace. Baked without air for a day or two in heaps or ovens, a suitable caking coal loses its tar and gas and part of its sulphur and becomes coke: hard, porous, nearly pure carbon. Coke carries a taller burden than charcoal, so furnaces can be much bigger, and it frees ironmaking from the forest. It needs a stronger blast (blowing cylinders driven by water or steam), more limestone to carry off the sulphur, and from 1828 a preheated blast that cut fuel use by about two thirds.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming any coal will do; many coals do not coke or hold too much sulphur, which makes the iron crack when forged hot.
  - Using charcoal-sized bellows; coke will not burn hot enough without a harder blast.
  - Saying Darby's 1709 success changed the industry at once; early coke pig was sold mainly for castings; widespread use for bar iron came later.
  - Coke ovens and coal gas contain carbon monoxide; men died sleeping beside warm ovens.
- History: china: 11th c. – Song ironworks in the north use coal on a large scale; coke is probable but the evidence is thin. Coal-fired crucible smelting is documented later; europe: 1709 – Abraham Darby, Coalbrookdale; general in Britain only from the 1750s; 1784 puddling makes coke pig into bar iron; 1828 Neilson's hot blast; americas: 1830s–1850s – anthracite and then coke furnaces in Pennsylvania; india: 1875 – first lasting coke blast furnace at Kulti (Bengal)
- Read:
  - Arthur Raistrick, Dynasty of Iron Founders: The Darbys and Coalbrookdale (1953)
  - Robert Hartwell, A Revolution in the Chinese Iron and Coal Industries during the Northern Sung, 960–1126 A.D., Journal of Asian Studies 21 (1962)
  - Joel Mokyr, The Lever of Riches (1990)
